speechtext:
In
view of the fact that the rediscount rate has been raised to 1\ per cent, as announced by the governor of the Bank of Canada, and in view of the effect this will have on interest rates generally, is the minister giving thought or will he give thought to the possibility of imposing some restraint on interest rates, bearing in mind that higher rates will increase costs and add to the inflationary spiral?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE BY BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
The bank rate in Canada was raised to follow the rediscount rate in the United States. It was evidence that Canada intends to maintain the value of the Canadian dollar. If we had not acted in this way I think our position would have been subject to misinterpretation. The purpose is to continue

March 15, 1968
Inquiries of the Ministry to attract capital into Canada in order to maintain the stability of the Canadian dollar and the Canadian economy. If we had not taken this action the result would have been serious. Therefore this is a contribution to employment, price stability and the general well being of the economy.

subtopic: INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE BY BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: In view of the fact that an increase in interest rates will increase costs and consequently add to inflation, is the minister considering any restraint to prevent interest rates generally from rising and avoid the disastrous effect this could produce by further escalating inflationary pressure on the economy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE BY BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: The only answer I am able to give is that I can think of nothing more serious than the instability of the Canadian dollar.

subtopic: INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE BY BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: Would the minister explain to the house why there is a 2 5 point spread in the so-called rediscount rate in Canada as compared to the United States, a spread which is much wider than is normally the case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE BY BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the difference between the rediscount rates in Canada and the United States is not really the significant figure. The really significant figure is the difference between long term interest rates in Canada and the United States. This is slightly above normal, but not very much.

subtopic: INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE BY BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: A further supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Would the minister explain why there will be this 1J point spread in the prime rate charged by the various banks as a result of the increase in the bank rate by Canada, which represents a 2J point spread?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE BY BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a reflection of the fundamental situation that exists in international markets today. This is one of the most disturbed periods we have had. I can only reiterate that I believe the measures that are being taken are essential to underline the importance of maintaining the stability of the Canadian dollar. I can think of nothing more useful to the stability of employment and the standard of living of Canadians than to defend the Canadian dollar at the present time.

subtopic: INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE BY BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I put a supplementary question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE BY BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the rate of interest in the market will be determined by the competitive forces that are at work, not only by the bank rate but by other factors as well. subtopic: INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE BY BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I put a further supplementary question? Could the minister tell us how it is that the Bank of Canada can increase its discount rate without consulting parliament which, after all, is sovereign in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE BY BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the government looks at all possible measures that will underpin the stability of the Canadian dollar in this very troubled world. speechtext:

Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Finance. I wonder if the minister could inform the house whether there is any intention to close the gold market in Canada, as has been done in Great Britain.

speechtext:
At the moment we are in the eye of the hurricane and no one knows exactly what is going to come out of it. Those of my age, sir, cannot help hearing ominous echoes of 1929. We can only hope that those who today are in charge of the international monetary system and the governments of the major industrial countries will exhibit more wisdom than their predecessors of some 40 odd years ago, who stood helplessly wringing their hands while the world slipped into disaster.
I am not too optimistic, sir, that this wisdom will be found, because for some years those same people have been dodging the real issue before us in the international monetary system; that is, the development of a new international unit of exchange. I should say at

March 15, 1968
Income Tax Act
this point that Canada's record on this is extremely good. We produced workable proposals for the development of such a unit, but they were frustrated by other nations in the world.
There are, of course, certain options open to the United States which would have their effect on Canada. No one can say yet what option the United States will take. One hears rumours of a two price system for gold, which strikes me as being difficult to work. It may be possible to make it work. One hears rumours that gold is to be demonetized. That would entail certain other actions on the part of the United States government which I doubt they are prepared to take at this time.
I think, in connection with this bill, we should turn our attention to what should be done to protect Canada's position. I will be frank to say, sir, that I was nothing short of appalled at the minister's answers to questions this morning. They indicate that he is locked in some sort of conventional wisdom and feels that the Canadian dollar can be protected indefinitely by the use of exchange reserves, despite the lamentable history of the same policy in the United Kingdom and the United States. I suggest to him, as I suggested the other day, that there is really only one way to protect the Canadian dollar, and that is by developing an expanding and prosperous economy in Canada.
I was disturbed, sir, to find the minister dismissing and rejecting out of hand the suggestions made in questions by the leader of this party and the member for York South, that steps should be taken to control the rise in interest rates and that measures ought to be taken to put into effect exchange controls. Frankly I consider the minister's answers ludicrous; sheer nonsense. I am afraid we will land ourselves in exactly the same sort of jam the world was landed in 40 years ago if the views of the minister and what he says are the views of the governor of the Bank of Canada are to be the views of those who control the international monetary system.
Finally, I suggest that this parliament ought to consider seriously the wisdom of recessing at this time. It may well become necessary to pass emergency legislation, and I doubt very much the wisdom of dismissing parliament now. We realize, of course, that to keep parliament in session at this time would be extremely awkward for the government party but surely, sir, the future of Canada and the possible necessity of taking drastic steps to protect ourselves from what may

come out of the international crisis ought to override any party consideration of convenience at this time.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR SURCHARGE
speechtext: I quite agree.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will say only a few words, in view of the serious crisis in the financial field and the gold rush that has been going on for some weeks and that brought about yesterday the closing of the stock exchange and banks in several countries of the world.
There is no mistake about it, in the light of present circumstances, we live in a world of madmen and we are administered by the most remarkable among them.
Those people are tripping over themselves while they rush to the golden calf, but workmen and farmers got up as usual this morning to go about their work. Indeed, the farmers got up at the usual time this morning, namely about four or five o'clock, to milk the cows. This reminds me of a statement I heard once, to the effect that farmers got up at four o'clock to milk their cows while financiers got up at ten o'clock to milk the farmers. That is somewhat the situation in which we find ourselves at the present time.
The price of milk did not go up this morning. The salary of workers did not improve. Yet, the financial system, by order of the Bank of Canada, raises its discount rate by one half of one per cent without resorting to parliament. The banks, as I said a while ago, will raise their rates again and the people will again be trampled underfoot by the system.
[DOT] (12 noon)
We all know the story of the tower of Babel where there was a great confusion of languages. This does not mean that people did not speak the same language, but they did not understand each other, and when they saw this, they stopped building the tower.
We are building another tower of Babel today. People in the same country, province or municipality do not understand one another. But the difference today is that we are too stupid to stop building this tower of Babel.
Mr. Speaker, for thirty yeears, the Creditistes have been warning the succeeding federal governments of the situation now existing. The Creditistes have been called everything. It has been said that the implementing of their theory would give rise to inflation, economic chaos, a total failure of our economy, the downfall of Canada.
March 15, 1968

Today, our country is on the brink of ruin. We are witnessing an unrestrained race for financial control, and Social Credit is not to blame. It is not Social Credit that created the present inflation. It is not Social Credit which is responsible for the rise in the cost of living or for the extravagant expenditures in all fields.
Mr. Speaker, if serious consideration had been given to the solutions advocated by Social Credit thirty years ago, namely that the currency should truly reflect our resources and our production, we would not have today to cope with the system or the situation imposed upon us by a small group of men.
As a matter of fact, Pius XI said in 1931, 37 years ago already: Those who control money and credit are the masters of our whole lives and, without their permission, nobody has the right to breathe.
Let us consider the present situation in Great Britain. Let us consider the extreme poverty generally prevailing throughout the world. Let us observe the people getting nervous, businessmen getting worried, industrialists hesitating to forge ahead, to take action. Why? Because those who control money and credit have the power to prevent them from breathing.
Moreover, Pope Pius XI said that economics will be established and will truly attain its purpose only when it will provide each and every one of us with a part of the goods that nature and industry can provide, and that part should be sufficient to ensure a decent living for each and every one of us.
That is the aim, those are the objectives of a well planned economy, an economy that is serving the population. The pope did not say: inasmuch as the financial system allows, he said: "Inasmuch as nature and industry allow".
Now, Mr. Speaker, nature allows Canada to produce overabundant goods of all kinds, and industry, which is continuously ready to second nature, should not be blocked nor impeded in the upward march towards progress, towards the emancipation of our people, in short it should not be thwarted by an outmoded financial system which makes for legalized robbery in most countries where it is used.
Those are, Mr. Speaker, the few considerations which I wanted to make on the motion for third reading of Bill No. C-208. That bill will not solve the problem, it will not bring relief to poverty in Canada and I am repeating what I said two days ago: even if that bill
Income Tax Act
provided a 25 per cent tax increase, it would not solve the situation in Canada.
It is not by taxing the labourer nor by overtaxing the small business or the small industry that we will save the Canadian economy, but by taking instead adequate monetary measures, some bold and courageous measures liable to put money at the disposal of the individual, not the individual at the disposal of money as expected in Bill No. C-208 which the government is attempting to have passed at this time.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to make only a few comments on the bill in the debate on third reading by way of adding to the remarks which have been made as to the seriousness of the situation we face. I think it behoves us in this house to dispense with this bill as soon as possible.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR SURCHARGE

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR SURCHARGE
speechtext: Yes. Dispense with it,

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR SURCHARGE
speechtext:
Although we cannot agree with its basic policy we understand very well the need to avoid precipitating a further crisis at home which might weaken the confidence of the public in the operation of the parliamentary system. By doing so we would only be adding to the pressures which are building up on the international scene.
Having said that, I would urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) to do his utmost to bring about in the future so far as international monetary policy is concerned a system different from that which has been in operation in the past. We have been hanging on to the ragged coat-tails of an outworn financial policy which should have been discarded long ago. Many Canadians today are confused about what really is behind the crisis which we and other nations are facing. What has gold to do with trade balances and international settlements? What has it to do with our own financial system in Canada? It is not easy to find answers to these questions but I am sure that if we did so we would realize that in the game of international finance and politics the Soviet union, France, Switzerland and possibly South Africa will come out of this situation best.
Unfortunately, the United States government has insisted on hanging on to a policy which has resulted in a fantastic rise in interest rates, one which has worked undue hardship

March 15, 1968
Income Tax Act
on us in Canada and placed a great strain on our economy and the stability of our finances. Because the United States has insisted on pegging the value of gold at an unrealistic level, pressure is now being exercised against the economic system in the world by countries which would destroy the policy which lias insisted on maintaining the American dollar as the basis of international exchange-I *am thinking of destruction in financial, not military terms.
The Minister of Finance owes it not only to his government but to his country to be in Washington to take part in the conferences scheduled for the weekend and insist we should no longer hang on to a financial system which could destroy the United States dollar as the medum of international exchange and take ours with it in the process. It is not enough to patch up the old arrangements. Before we see a repetition of what happened in 1929 a real effort must be made to restore confidence among the people of the world and to devise a system of exchange and international settlements which will remove once and for all the dangers which threaten the security of everyone in the world today. Canada has the opportunity to take the lead and insist that although something needs to be done so far as gold is concerned for a temporary period, it is necessary in the long run to devise a new system of international settlements designed to avoid a repetition in the future of the kind of crisis we are facing today.

We in this corner of the house, believe that we must deal immediately with the third reading of this bill whether or not we like the policies contained therein. I think that the Minister of Finance must take the major share of the blame for our present difficulties, but it is imperative that we do not add further to the uncertainty and lack of confidence that are developing in financial circles. Beyond this it is also necessary that steps be taken-and I suggest Canada could well take the lead-to bring about a new international exchange system which would not continually lead us into the precarious position that has been forced upon us by the present international situation.

speechtext: Order, please. House again in committee of supply. Estimates of the Department of the Secretary of State, vote No. 2c. Shall vote 2c carry?
2c. Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment-National Arts Centre, $7,500,000.

Last night, Mr. Chairman, some comments were made about the Secretary of State, the member for Niagara Falls, and her contribution last year to centennial year. I wish to add my compliments to those which have been given. No one could have been more generous than the minister in the way she used her time and energy in making the many appearances she made last year, nor could anyone else have shown greater co-operation to the thousands of people interested in promoting centennial undertakings.

Hear, hear.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)

Just before ten o'clock last night the hon. member for Timiskaming expressed the concern that many of us feel about the length of time it is taking to build the National Arts Centre. I believe that most Canadians were pleased when the project was

initiated. However, since its initial introduction many have become concerned about construction delays and many have expressed concern to me about the additional costs that are being incurred, which have been partly brought about by delays in building and partly by other causes. According to the auditor's report for 1967 the cost of construction was $6,400,000, an increase of $2,800,000 over the preceding year, a substantial rise of some 25 per cent. According to the supplementary estimates, under the item for construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment there is an amount of $7,500,000, a further sharp increase. From the few figures I have come across in these records the total seems to be about $17,500,000 and we have heard various rumours that the cost will eventually go as high as $60 million or $70 million.
Can the minister tell the committee the size of the original estimate for the construction of the National Arts Centre and at what point the government intends to put a lid upon these skyrocketing costs? I might add that they do not include administrative and operating costs which are listed separately at $1,100,000, an increase of $80,000 over last year.

Mr. Chairman, there were questions asked last night about the National Arts Centre, especially with respect to the critical path. I have checked with the Department of Public Works which, as hon. members know, is responsible for construction, and I am told that the critical path method is being used. There is one man specifically in charge. It is my understanding that progress is on time; the project is to be completed and turned over on the last day of this year. It will then take three or four months to try out the auditorium. The original plan was that in May, 1969, productions would be staged, and as far as we are aware everything is on time. Of course, we do not know whether there will be any major strikes in the intervening period.
So far as costs are concerned it is my recollection, and I have not refreshed my memory recently, that the first estimate for the building amounted to some $18 million. My information is that the latest estimate, now about two years old, of a figure around $40 million or $43 million, represents what the cost will be, right on target.
The figures which appear each year for the administration of the centre increase, of course, as we approach the day when programs are to begin. The site is not very
March 15, 1968	COMMONS
attractive now and it certainly was not attractive throughout the centennial year, but it seems to me hon. members are not really aware of how much has been completed inside the building. I have been remiss in this respect but after the remarks made last night I discussed this matter with the Minister of Public Works, and with his concurrence I am pleased to invite any member of the House of Commons who may wish to go for a guided tour of the premises at 11.30 a.m. on Monday next. A great deal of the building is like an iceberg. It has to be seen to be believed and I think that if hon. members would take an hour of their time to look at it they would appreciate how large an enterprise it is.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: In issuing this invitation is the hon. lady suggesting that we should allow her estimates to stand until we have seen the building?

Not at all. This building will be the heart of Ottawa when it is opened about a year from now and I made my offer because I think hon. members would like an opportunity to see it. After all, it is a national centenary project and it is well ahead of many of other centenary projects, notably the one sponsored by the province of Ontario which is not expected to reach completion until a year later.
The board of trustees was set up more than a year ago and has held regular meetings, as have a great many auxiliary committees. It is working now in connection with the programs to be presented. Already it has been announced that Stratford Theatre is to become the Stratford National Theatre and will operate from the centre during the winter. There is to be a French speaking company to complement this arrangement and a concert orchestra which can be used as a pit orchestra; it will also be used by the C.B.C. for some of its functions and will be available to increase cultural activity within the city. Running costs are increasing because these plans have to be made in advance. One cannot produce an orchestra by May, 1969 in the absence of time for preparation.
I believe that if hon. members would take advantage of the opportunity to visit the buildings under construction, wearing hard hats and clothes which will not spoil too easily, bearing in mind that work is still in progress, they will have a new sense of pride in what will be a considerable national monument.

Supply-Secretary of State
I have a few other comments to make and perhaps this is a good opportunity to deal with other matters which have been raised. I should like to thank hon. members for their overly generous words both last night and today. I should particularly like to thank the hon. lady who sits for Grenville-Dundas for her contribution to the centennial year, one of the most important of which was to pair with me on so many occasions, making it possible for me to be present at events in a non-political way. I think the hon. lady recognized, as did everyone else, that centenary projects were not party matters. All of us were careful not to bring partisan politics into them and it was an occasion for considerable pride for both of us that we were able to show our non-partisan approach by appearing together for most of the year.
It was a happy circumstance that the work of members of the Centennial Commission should have been mentioned in the discussions last night. The commission yesterday held its last meeting. Most of the employees have been re-engaged elsewhere, though some have not yet found positions. We expect all the work to be closed down on March 31, on which date the commission will go out of existence. In this connection I have a rather important announcement to make. It is the only one of its kind, I think, I have had to make in the seven and a half years I have been in parliament and one in which the committee of supply should be interested. The Centennial Commission instructed me yesterday that it is turning back to the treasuo' some $3,400,000 in unexpended funds.

I have one other question regarding the National Arts Centre. It relates to the future and has to do with advertising. Has the minister any plans with respect to general promotion of the centre's activities? I would refer in the first place to a magazine called Prologue which has been sent to me. Apparently it is being sent out broadly; it is stated on page one that the purpose of Prologue is to let Canadians everywhere know about the National Arts Centre. Apparently there are to be six issues sent out before the centre opens and I have been asked to find out what sending it to Canadians everywhere means, how many copies are to be distributed and what the approximate cost will be.

I do not have this information. I shall be glad to get it and send it to the hon. member. I am not familiar with the particular issue mentioned, but one of the objects of the trustees is to work with the
7680	COMMONS
Supply-Secretary of State Canada Council to make the centre a focus for all Canadians. It is important that people outside the capital city should have a sense of engagement and with this in mind it is desirable that they should know what is going on.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to echo the remarks made by the charming and gracious member for Grenville-Dun-das and praise the good work of the Secretary of State during centennial year. I should like to say, too, that I believe the Centennial Commission did a fine job. If I may, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one particular comment. I think that much is owed to John Fisher, the man who taught us all that our Canadianism should show. I think he should not be forgotten.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
I should also like to thank the hon. lady for her invitation for next Monday. It will not be too much trouble to find clothes that are not so good, to use her expression. All I need is a hard hat size 7fths and I shall be with her. I too am anxious to see the National Arts Centre commence business. Although I welcome it, I think the point raised by my colleague is extremely important and is something that should concern not only the minister but all ministers, indeed all parliamentarians.
These are very difficult times. Parliamentary institutions and the whole process of government are in disrepute, or near disrepute. One constantly hears increasing reaction along the line that whatever the government attempts to do it does it badly or it does not do it in time or it does it at too high a cost. I think this is something that we must watch. Buildings are not completed on time and the estimates are far removed from the actual cost. Therefore in these difficult and questioning times when people are looking askance at their institutions-and in a democracy the bulk of the people must respect the political institutions in order for them to work-all of us, especially those in executive authority, must look at matters such as the escalated cost of this building, which should cause to the most art-minded person in Canada to worry.
I would compliment the minister on her optimism and on her felicity of expression when she suggested that this building will be completed on time when actually it will be completed on the last day of the year following centennial year. We must remember that in fact it was a centennial project. However, it does us no good to harp on the past. The
[Miss LaMarsh.l

Mr. Chairman, I only have a very brief question for the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh), relating to vote lc.
As regards the $100,000 grant to Le centre culturel du vieux Montreal, can she tell us whether this is the same theatrical company that went bankrupt recently and that was quartered in the stock exchange building? Yes, I think that was the name. Can the minister tell us whether the grant will be allowed nonetheless?
Yes.

So, it is the same theatrical company? I would like to make a comment. The minister tells me that this $100,000 will nonetheless be granted to this company. The hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Boulanger) tells me the company is back on its feet thanks to this grant.
The creditors accepted the company's offer and everything is all right now.

So much the better, if that means they have ben able to resume their activities.
Mr. Chairman, vote 2c reads as follows:
Construction or Acquisition of Buildings, Works, Land and Equipment-National Arts Centre.
I wish to put a question to the hon. minister concerning another building which was promised a long time ago and which is not progressing very fast-the C.B.C. building in Montreal. Could the hon. minister tell us what progress has been made and when we can expect that building to be finished? Could she give us some information concerning the C.B.C. building in Montreal?

Mr. Chairman, I was in communication with Mr. Davidson, the new president of the C.B.C., the other day. He had asked that this along with other matters be held over until he had had time to look into them. He is having a meeting of the new board some time around the end of April at which time he will be prepared to make submissions to the board in regard to the Montreal building. We have every hope that after
March 15, 1968

the new board has met tenders will be called almost immediately and construction will go ahead.

lc. Administration, production and distribution of films and other visual materials, $170,000.

Mr. Chairman, I have two or three brief comments on this item and also one proposal. I think the film board performs a very useful and rather underrated service to Canada. I am told that at least 16 million people in Canada see one production or another of the film board every year and that 30 million people in other countries see productions of the National Film Board. The quality of the N.F.B. productions is indicated by the fact that over recent years more than 600 international awards have been won by the National Film Board for its work.
The work of the board is not confined simply to the production of films. Some of its employees are working on improvements in technical equipment which may be very useful. The board also plays a useful role in helping various departments of government by illustrating their efforts. In this regard I think the film board is to be commended.
The proposal I want to make and draw particularly to the attention of the Secretary of State, if I may, concerns what seems to me to be an urgent need for some action at the federal level to preserve historic Canadian film. Two or three archive organizations in this country are trying to do something along that line but I believe that they are not receiving sufficient financial support from the Canadian public. The film that the Canadian Film Institute is trying to preserve is irreplaceable. It is old film having to do with the earliest beginnings of the Canadian film industry. It is a sad fact to relate that last year a million feet of this historic film was burned because it was insecurely stored. In concluding my remarks I take the opportunity to direct the attention of the Secretary of State to this problem and to urge her to do what she can to draw together those connec-ed with film archives to see whether or not they can work out with federal aid a program that will really protect historic Canadian film.

Mr. Chairman, I have a question I want to ask the Secretary of State in connection with the National Film Board. In all my dealings with government organizations I have never found a department of government performing its functions more
27053-484^
Supply-Secretary of State adequately and perfectly than the film board. During the last 15 years I have had direct connections with the board and have arranged to purchase from them many hundreds of dollars worth of film which we have distributed to boards of education and school trustees for use in the school system of Ontario. The coverage given by the National Film Board to historical events, geographical features and industrial complexes is perfect.
However, in view of the uproar that is developing over educational television, which is something that leaves me cold-I am in favour of education through the use of film because you can use film when you want-I should like to ask the minister what proportion of the sales of the National Film Board is to school boards and boards of education for use in classroom instruction under the jurisdiction of the boards of education. These films are perfect for this purpose. I should like to think that all of their sales are made in this field, but what proportion is sold for educational purposes?
Mr. Chairman, I am afraid I could not even hazard a guess but I will get the information as soon as I can.

Mr. Chairman, I raise the question only to emphasize the wonderful work that the National Film Board is doing in the field of visual education. The way it covers visual education cannot be improved upon by television because it is adequately presented in film form. The National Film Board is showing the way in this regard.
* (3:00 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I am rising briefly to support the representation by the hon. member for New Westminster that every effort be made to make certain that historic films be preserved in the future and are not subject to fire and destruction as has been the situation in a few cases in the past.
On behalf of a good many women in my riding who are associated with groups such as the women's institute and the parent-teachers association I should like to express their appreciation of the work done by the National Film Board in constituencies such as the one I have the honour to represent. There are many very small and sometimes isolated communities which have received very good service from the National Film Board. One of the best supporters of the National Film Board has been one of the finest national film councils of rural Canada, that of Kootenay West. I have been asked by these people to
March 15. 1968

Supply-Secretary of State express to the minister their appreciation of the good work done by the National Film Board in the area I represent.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to join with my colleagues in commending the work which the National Film Board has done over the years. It has produced a tremendous number of films of a cultural and educational .nature. These films have been shown not only to millions of people in Canada but to audiences all over the world. The excellence of the work done has been demonstrated again and again by the large number of international awards which the film board has received.
I join with other members of this group in commending the film board for the work it has been doing and in the hope that its work will be continued and extended.
I wish to raise a matter which while it may not be directly connected with the National Film Board is very close to it. I have reference to the Canadian Film Development Corporation. The bill which we discussed in 196667 was a proposal by the former secretary of state who is now a member of the other place that the people of Canada through the government co-operate in helping, through the creation of a fund, to establish in Canada a feature film industry. Although we are all aware of the work done by the National Film Board and the success it has had, Canada has not had a feature film industry despite the fact that in the English speaking world a number of Canadians have reached the top in the film industry as producers, writers, directors and actors. Great Britain, the United States and France are filled with ex-Canadians who are giving leadership and occupying important and influential places in the film industry.
It was the belief of the former secretary of state that we should endeavour to keep people such as these in Canada, a belief which I believe was shared by virtually everyone in this house. When the present Secretary of State brought forth the proposal to establish the Canadian Film Development Corporation and to provide a fund of $10 million she had virtually unanimous support. I should like to quote one paragraph from the statement of the minister on June 20, 1966 as recorded on page 6632 of Hansard. She said:
We should, Mr. Chairman, be under no illusion about the difficulties which Canadian producers will face in building up a commercially viable industry in this country. They will have to make it commercially viable by exporting their work, which will have to be done by virtue of profitable


distribution arrangements. Canadian films must prove good enough to win their own place on world screens.
I could quote further from the remarks of the minister on that and other occasions, but I believe we realized at that time as we do now that while this is an idea worthy of our support it will not be easy to buck the giants of the United States and Great Britain in the production of feature length films. It is very seldom that such films can be produced for a small amount of money. The government of Canada has provided a fund of $10 million. Most of us would like to see that money used to good advantage over a period of time.
Yesterday the names of the appointees to the board of directors of this corporation were announced. I should like to advise the minister, if she has not heard this already, that many members of parliament including myself are dismayed by the appointments which have been made. In addition every person in and around the film industry to whom I have spoken since yesterday is dismayed. Although the board is a very estimable group of ladies and gentlemen, with the possible exception of Madame Favreau they have had virtually no experience in the film industry and are all good Liberals. While these are not necessarily bad features I submit that they have nothing to do with the qualities required to make a success of this corporation.
I do not object to the government of Canada being generous and spending $40 million, as was mentioned a few moments ago, to build a performing arts centre and I do not mind the federal government making a contribution to agriculture-I will always support that. The whole purpose of this corporation, however, was to help finance and establish a commercial film industry. This is a very difficult, complicated and risky business. Here we find the government, on the recommendation of the minister, appointing a group of Liberal hacks as directors of the corporation. I have nothing against these persons as individuals. Mr. LaPalme, so far as I can ascertain, was a little better than average minister of the crown but he certainly is not expert in the field of the production of films. It is true that Mr. Frith has been a member of the B and B Commission and I believe he had some film-makers or television stations as clients in his law practice. Mr. Phillips and Mr. Harris were successful businessmen. They are also very influential members of the Liberal party. Madame Favreau has worked
March 15, 1968

for a number of years for the film board and has been a film critic for La Presse.
If it was a good idea for the government to put up a substantial amount of money in 1966 to help create a feature film industry in Canada so that Canadian producers, writers and directors would remain in Canada, surely it is a good idea now and, if so, we should do everything possible to see that this corporation is a success. The first thing we should not do is appoint a group of hacks as a reward for past political services, because the running of this corporation will be difficult under the best of circumstances. I see the minister looking at me with some concern or perhaps disdain. There are a number of ex-Canadians who have built fine reputations in these fields. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond on an earlier occasion talked about some Canadians who had gone on to make real names for themselves in this field, including Norman Jewison, Sydney Newman, Graeme Ferguson and Sydney Furie. These are individuals who have been eminently successful in making films which have not only been artistic and cultural but financially successful. These are the kind of people the minister ought to be looking for to be directors of this corporation, not such people as have been appointed so far.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I can only say to the minister in closing my brief remarks that I could not help but think, as I looked at the announcement of the appointments, that the only appointments that have been as bad or worse since I came to Ottawa are the appointments the present Prime Minister has made to the other place.

Mr. Chairman, I have to answer these remarks because I disagree totally with what the hon. member has said. He is obviously not aware of what this board is, because it is intended to be a bank. It is a board where money will be raised in a number of different ways, by grants, loans and participation. It will have a package responsibility in respect of scripts, star arrangements, distribution and everything else. We have been through all this. This is not to be a group that necessarily knows how to make movies because it will not make movies. This is to be a group that is culturally oriented and prepared to act in regard to a banking situation. There is to be a full time director who will be an expert in at least one of the aspects of movie-making.
Supply-Secretary of State
I was very intrigued by the comparison which was made between members of this board and two or three gentlemen now living and working abroad who were originally Canadians and have now made their marks in the film industry. Most of them are drawing salaries of the nature of $100,000 a year. It is really laughable when my hon. friend suggests that we should somehow divorce them from their various enterprises in Italy, California and Britain to bring them back here for the kind of pittance this country pays its public servants. It is all very well to stand and make that kind of N.D.P. speech, but it has no practicality.
When it comes to setting up a board I am not prepared to appoint hacks, and while I know lots of hacks in lots of parties in the country I would not qualify any of the individuals on this board in that way. The chairman of the board is one of the most distinguished sons of French Canada. He is not only a very distinguished lawyer but also was the first Quebec minister of cultural affairs and one who felt so deeply about the field of cultural affairs that he resigned his portfolio because he did not think the province of Quebec was putting sufficient money into the field. I am quite astounded that the hon. member or anyone else would suggest that this gentleman, who has been good enough to accept this appointment, is a party hack. This man was good enough to be appointed by the mayor of Montreal, in respect of whom every party has tried to make claims, as his cultural adviser for the son of Expo. Surely no one can suggest that this man is a party hack, particularly in view of the amount of time he has generously offered us in the first year. This will be fairly onerous for this part time member of a federal board. It will amount to about a day per week.
I do not personally know the lady appointee but she comes very highly recommended. I do not know what her politics are and I have never inquired. She does have a particular qualification that recommends itself to me in that she happens to be female. I wanted a particularly good bilingual female on this board and this young woman seems to qualify.
Having regard to Mr. Frith, who is now living in this city, it is true that he has been a follower of the Liberal party. I for one do not find anything wrong with that, but he has not held office for eight or nine years and has been engaged in a number of enterprises,
March 15, 1968

Supply-Secretary of State almost all of them in the cultural field, including television and radio. He was one of the most distinguished and hard-working members of the B and B commission and is one individual who above all others in the country is dedicated to a belief in the flourishing two founding cultures of Canada.
I met Mr. Phillips of Vancouver once. I believe he is a Liberal although I do not think he has particularly identified himself as such. Perhaps he will deny that he is. I am informed that he has made investments in films made in Canada, the latest being made by the British industry and starring Rita Tushingham. It was shown a year or so ago on the west coast. He is an enterprising and vigorous young businessman who knows what it is to invest his own money in this field. This seems to me to be a good background when it comes to investing public money.
Having regard to Mr. Harris, I do not know him personally but have been informed that he has a very distinguished career in business. I have never heard that he has any politics. He is a man who is particularly interested in the arts and the theatre.
It strikes me that all these people are particularly cultivated and well qualified Canadians. The most anyone can say is that they have taken an active interest in the affairs of their country and have chosen the best party to support. By no stretch of any rational kind of imagination could any of them be called a hack.

I do not know whether it was by accident or by design that the minister neglected to comment on Mr. Elliott, who is also a member of the board. Let me refer to the minister's own press release which indicates that Mr. Elliott, after working for a number of Ontario newspapers, joined the MacLaren advertising agency of Toronto in 1948. It is stated that he served six years as film production supervisor in the agency's television department and is now a vice president and director of the company. There is not much purpose in pursuing the political aspects but I want to put on record, in case the minister is as unknowledgeable about politics as she seems to be, that other members of this house know about the close relationship between the Liberal party and the MacLaren agency. It is not an accident that this gentleman was appointed to the board.
Surely I made it clear in my earlier remarks that I exempted Madame Favreau from my suggestion. I said she had spent a number of years working at the film board and as film critic for La Presse.
[Miss LaMarsh.l

I accept the minister's word that these people are interested in culture, but that is not the point. They have not been appointed as directors of the C.B.C. or as directors of the National Film Board, both of which are concerned to a large extent with educational and cultural productions. They have been appointed to a corporation with the one purpose of co-financing, which was the term I think the minister used when introducing the legislation, commercial full length films.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I say to the minister, as she said then, that this is a difficult and risky business. I hoped we would do everything possible to see that this business is a success. It is true, as the minister says, that these people will be acting as sort of directors of a bank. I have not had the experience with banks of some hon. members but I am quite sure that if you went to the Royal Bank of Canada, the Bank of Montreal or any other bank, or one of the banks we have established such as the Industrial Development Bank, the person with whom you would deal if you wanted money in large quantities would be one who had a pretty good grasp of all the implications of the business in which the prospective borrower was interested. If you want to borrow money for building houses you will deal with somebody in a bank who knows about building houses. If you want to borrow money for building a factory you will deal with somebody who knows what are the prospects of the industry concerned.
I suggest that there should have been appointed to the board as directors people who know the film industry. With regard to the people I mentioned, I forget the minister's exact term but she said my suggestion was ludicrous and so on because they are making $100,000 a year. That is true. Because they can make that kind of money and are successful I suggest they are the kind of people who should have been appointed to this board. I think it would be wonderful if one of them could come back to Canada as the full time general manager of the corporation, but here we have a part time board and I presume the members will be paid only an honorarium and their expenses. I am reasonably certain that amongst the names I have mentioned and hundreds I could mention who have left Canada to be actors, producers and directors there are two or three who would have been honoured had the minister said to them: Would you sit on a board of directors
March 15, 1968

to help us establish a film industry in Canada? I am sure many of them feel they owe a debt of gratitude to this country for the start we gave them in the C.B.C., and so on. I am sure some of them could have been persuaded to sit on this board of directors rather than the kind of people the minister has appointed.

Mr. Chairman, I did make one oversight with regard to Mr. Elliott. Mr. Elliott has had some experience, as was indicated, with respect to films. He is one of the most brilliant young men it has been my pleasure to meet. Indeed, at one point there was a very strong chance that he would be nominated as the film commissioner for the National Film Board. He was not, however, in a position to devote full time attention to the public service. I apologize to Mr. Elliott for not dealing with him in the list to which I referred and which I had committed to memory.
However, the hon. member should realize that a number of people who have made an impression internationally in the film field are extremely interested in this program and have been writing me over the past couple of years because they wanted to know when the board of directors would be set up so they could make a proposition and obtain money from the board. Almost everyone I have spoken to throughout Canada who has been potentially a person who might serve on the board has had to demur when I have told him or her that they would, of course, completely and legally have to disassociate themselves from any enterprise which would at any time make any claim on the fund of $10 million. This has been the situation in the case of the best known home-grown Canadian film talent, who would have had to leave their companies in order to become associated with this board, as well as in the case of some who are not as well known. A great many people who were interested in and eager to take part in the program, once they realize that the proprieties of the situation were such that they could not have any financial interest of any kind and serve on the board, decided to stay away from the board and at a later time make application in the hope that they would be able to make Canadian films.
The hon. member cannot have it both ways. He suggests that if you go to a bank and want to borrow money in order to participate in a particular enterprise you go to someone in the bank who is qualified to deal with that matter. That is exactly what we hope will happen in
Supply-Secretary of State respect of this board, namely, that if you go to the film development corporation you will be speaking to people who have an active knowledge of the industry and are there as full time appointees. A decision will be made by the board of trustees. This is exactly the same situation as obtains with the board of trustees of any bank, which is certainly not made up of people who do not understand the situation that exists when you ask for a loan.
I have noticed in this post, as in others I have held in the last couple of years, that when I have made nominations of appointees to positions my enemies, and sometimes my friends, have put forward arguments about appointing supporters of my party simply because they are supporters. I state quite frankly that the pressure in this regard is becoming less and less. But if I see two people before me and they are both good I will pick a Liberal any time over the other applicant. I make no apology for doing this.
It also seems to me that when we set up a board like this with respect to something that will be difficult but interesting, we are approaching very closely the American system whereby the day after the announcement is made there is in this house an unprincipled attack on the people appointed, even before they have picked a staff and opened an office. I suggest to the committee that they wait until the next supplementary estimates are presented to make these criticisms. I also suggest that the hon. member, in his generosity of heart and mind, should stand up and swallow his words.

Mr. Chairman, I assure the minister that if a year from now I see that this corporation is doing a good job I shall, regardless of what I have said-and I retract nothing I have said up to now-make a special point of rising and commending the board for so doing even though they are laymen, which makes it difficult. But I say to the minister that I speak not only for myself but for a number of people in and around this field who are interested in the matter. I have spoken to some of these people since I saw the announcement in the press yesterday, and they expressed in even more vigorous language than I have their views in this regard. I could not use their language here because it would, to say the least, be unparliamentary.

Mr. Chairman, I am among those who are somewhat surprised at the attitude of our colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). I know him well enough to know that he is incapable of a mean action or a shallow judgment. If I did not know him, I would be inclined to accuse him of pettiness in the circumstances, since he just gave an opinion which is not based -according to his own comments-on definite facts.
I sincerely believe that the minister does not have to make any apology to the house for her choice as concerns the appointment of the members of that board.
Personally, I cannot, without protest, let anyone make comments reflecting, for instance, on the integrity and the competence of Mr. Georges-Emile Lapalme. I have had the good fortune of knowing him intimately for a great number of years. I had the opportunity of seeing him perform in all kinds of fields. I also had the opportunity of ascertaining the soundness of his judgment, the confidence he inspires around him in all artistic circles, whether the graphic arts, the drama or any other artistic field.
In the province of Quebec, he has been a sort of innovator in all artistic fields. In fact, he has been called upon in all kinds of circles, including the provincial fields and those that are free from partisan politics. The municipal authorities of the city of Montreal, for instance, and the organizers of certain symphony concerts and such have repeatedly called upon his assistance. I say that he is a man of irreproachable judgment, known intellectual integrity and honesty, and very sound artistic taste.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, I know Miss Favreau by reputation. I know her for having read personally a good number of her columns on artistic matters; I think I know her well enough to say that she is very objective in her comments. I know, of course, that it is a grievous fault if she, or the others, are Liberals. Had sympathizers of the New Democratic party or the Ralliement Creditiste or the Conservatives been chosen, this would probably have won them favour, but still, that is the game of politics and, to my mind, it should not be taken into account.
But the point my hon. friend from Winnipeg North failed to see is that people in the business are not necessarily sought out for such agencies. It is rather a matter of creating a

body which will know how to distribute, as equitably as possible, while observing the rules of distributive justice, that amount of $10 million the government is making available to those who will be willing to expand the film industry in Canada. Are technical people really needed for that purpose? Of course not, and on that point, I disagree with my friend for Winnipeg North.
Mr. Chairman, it so happens that a technician in the film making business has necessarily belonged to a particular school of thought and has been prompted by his personal taste and habits, for a great many years. If, by the force of circumstances, he is asked to sit on such a board, he should not allow himself to be influenced by his personal tastes, tendencies and habits, by his friends of many years or by the school which helped him to make a name for himself. If such types of persons are necessarily sought, it is quite reasonable to think that, at times, they may lack objectivity.
In such a case, we have chosen-at least, so I presume, because I am not acquainted with the others-businessmen who know how to administer a budget, people who have enough common sense and refined artistic taste, to know how to distribute that money, without necessarily giving too much to one school or one movement, but who will give to all those who can enrich the Canadian heritage in the film industry.
Now, Mr. Chairman, while pointing out those facts, I wish to say to the minister that she does not have to make any apology, especially if the remarks of my hon. friend for Winnipeg North have reflected on the reputation or prestige of Mr. Georges-Emile Lapalme. I would have liked to have tried to remedy the situation. I am sure that, a year or two from now, we will realize that we have an agency which is entirely capable of providing the country with the kind of service which it has been asked to provide.
Personally, I have complete confidence in the chairman of that agency. I cannot say anything about the other members, because I do not know them, but I believe that those who chose them certainly did not intend to choose election organizers, but people who will be an asset in the field of arts, and who will provide responsible management.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I have a question for the hon. minister.

In order to avoid any delay I will put my question in English. I understand that this $10
March 15, 1968	COMMONS
million will be distributed to those in the industry who will make films. Is it the intention of the minister or of the cabinet that this money eventually be reimbursed to the government in one way or another? Suppose a film is made, is then sold and makes a large profit. Will the grant allotted eventually be reimbursed to the government?

The legislation makes it clear that the board members may decide to invest in such a way as to have a share in any profits. Let us hope there is a share in the profits and not in the losses. It may also be that a grant may be given or even a straight loan with or without interest. It is certainly not the intention that the $10 million be completely spent. It is hoped that it will be a revolving fund and that profits will be forthcoming.

Mr. Chairman, before the item carries I wonder whether I could ask the minister a question. Would she undertake to give consideration to urging that new action be taken at the federal level for the preservation of historic films and the establishment of an adequate Canadian film archives to house irreplaceable art films?

A couple of years ago, when I undertook this portfolio, I was visited by representatives of various art groups. I asked them to meet and make a proposal as to who should keep the archives and who should have control of them. They have never come back to me with such a proposal. However, the film board keeps some film records, both in Montreal and in other regional centres, and of course the C.B.C. keeps a great number of them. I think it would be very helpful to the country if we had a central place in which to keep them. This is certainly something in which the film board is interested, and individual members of the film board such as Mr. Cote are very anxious to see it done.
I do not know whether in the next year's estimates the board will find some money to develop this program, but I think hon. members should realize there have been cut-backs and as of this week all agencies will have to take a 2 per cent cut. So while there is a continuing interest it may be that this year not much money will be spent on archives.

Just before the item carries I should like to ask the Secretary of State one question. It arises from inquiries I have received from persons interested in the Canadian Film Development Corporation and

Supply-Secretary of State the function it will have in promoting a feature film industry in Canada. Could the minister give the house any indication of how soon the corporation and its new board will be in a position to entertain applications for and inquiries about assistance to specific groups interested in launching themselves in the feature film industry? Is the board in a position to entertain such applications now?

No, Mr. Chairman. The new chairman who has just been appointed intends to call a meeting quite shortly. 1 have a list of almost 30 people with varying degrees of experience who have applied for the post of general manager of the board, and while this appointment is made by order in council it is made on the recommendation of the board. I should like to ask the minister a question on this item. Perhaps I am out of order but I will try the question on for size because she is in such an amiable green mood today. Is the government giving any consideration to having some form of regular review of the various pieces of legislation which deal with our relations with public service employees? speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I defended the main estimates of the department when the department was under the Registrar General last fall. There was also a very thorough debate on the new consumer branch when the consumer and corporate affairs re-organization bill was brought before the house in November and December. Perhaps it would be more practicable if hon. members would direct my attention to whatever subjects they would like discussed. I feel we have had a fairly full review of the department within the last two or three months. I am willing to make a statement but I think it might be more useful if members of the committee were to direct my attention to specific subjects.

Earlier today I raised a point with the minister and while I shall not labour it, it seems to me that a situation has developed in this country with regard to one of our national sports that deserves more consideration in parliament than it has received so far. I believe that thanks largely, I suspect, to the lure of television money, two hockey organizations in Canada have conspired against the national interest of Canadians. I refer to the Toronto Maple Leafs and the Montreal Canadiens. These two organizations have conspired to see to it that a third city in Canada shall be denied a franchise in the National Hockey League.
We have taken enough batting around of our national pride as a result of sending inferior hockey teams abroad to represent this country in so-called amateur play. In addition, however, we find a situation that has never been satisfactorily explained, namely, that ten of the 12 professional hockey teams on the North American continent are located in United States cities. The thought that immediately came to my mind with regard to the situation in Canada was that Toronto or Montreal, or both together, were unwilling to give up their share of the revenue that could be derived from national
March 15, 1968

television broadcasting in Canada and that they had their eye on the almighty buck instead of any national pride in this country.
As the minister said earlier today, perhaps this is a matter that we cannot study in this house. However, I suggest to him that there may be very good reasons why the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission or other groups that we have set up in days gone by should be looking at this situation to see whether we cannot get Vancouver a franchise. The Restrictive Trade Practices Commission appeals to me because when we examine the motives of the Toronto and Montreal people who made the decision to support United States interests rather than British Columbia interests I believe it is apparent that they were motivated by whatever cash could be divided between them rather than any other reason.
I hope the minister will be aggressive enough in the field of national interest and Canadian pride to take a look at this situation. I suggest to the hon. gentleman, whom I esteem highly as do many other members on this side, that this might be just the crowbar that would open the door to success in connection with certain events early in April here in Ottawa. This might be just the thing that would bring him through with flying colours, assisted by Canadian pride and assisted by decisions that were made behind closed doors by a self-interested, money-grasping group of people. If there is an ounce of sportsmanship in that group I will grant it but I think it is 99 per cent self-interest. There may be a 1 per cent interest in Canada's ability to develop the greatest hockey players in the world.

He referred to the fact we are sending inferior hockey teams abroad. If this remark were to stand without any further comment I think it might cast a reflection upon the Canadian national hockey team. I believe that the building of this hockey team is something which the theory the hon. member was advocating would assist. I feel that those who are behind these men have done much work which is in the country's interest. I know that in Newfoundland, from which one member of the team came,
